title: Nehemiah 11:1–24
context: To repopulate Jerusalem, the leaders live in the city and the people cast lots to bring one in ten to live there, while volunteers are blessed. The list of Jerusalem’s residents from Judah, Benjamin, the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in 11:3–19 has a parallel in 1 Chronicles 9:2–17, which differs in several names and numbers; the differences are noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: The princes of the people lived in Jerusalem. The rest of the people also cast lots to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem, the holy city, and nine parts in the other cities.
verses.arminianNotes: The leaders live in Jerusalem, and the people cast lots “to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem, the holy city.” Arminian readers see sacrifice for the sake of strengthening the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lot used to share a difficult responsibility. Jerusalem is called “the holy city,” emphasizing its importance as the place of God’s house.

verses.text: The people blessed all the men who willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “The people blessed all the men who willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see voluntary commitment honored by the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see willing service recognized and blessed. Readers in this tradition note that the verse leaves open how the volunteers related to those chosen by lot in verse 1.

verses.text: Now these are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the cities of Judah, everyone lived in his possession in their cities—Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the children of Solomon’s servants.
verses.arminianNotes: The chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem are introduced, while others lived in Judah’s cities. Arminian readers see a careful record of the community’s settlement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list beginning, as the chiefs of the province take their place in the city. Both traditions read the verse as a careful record of who lived in Jerusalem, without resolving differences from parallel lists.

verses.text: Some of the children of Judah and of the children of Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. Of the children of Judah: Athaiah the son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalalel, of the children of Perez;
verses.arminianNotes: Some of Judah and Benjamin live in Jerusalem, beginning with Athaiah of the children of Perez. Arminian readers see families from the tribe of Judah taking up residence in the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Judah’s line represented. The genealogy traces Athaiah to Perez, connecting the residents with the tribal history of Judah.

verses.text: and Maaseiah the son of Baruch, the son of Colhozeh, the son of Hazaiah, the son of Adaiah, the son of Joiarib, the son of Zechariah, the son of the Shilonite.
verses.arminianNotes: Maaseiah son of Baruch, descended from the Shilonite, is listed. Arminian readers see another branch of Judah represented among Jerusalem’s residents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a careful genealogy. Readers in this tradition note that “Shilonite” may refer to a clan of Judah rather than to the town of Shiloh, though the sense is debated.

verses.text: All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.
verses.arminianNotes: “All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.” Arminian readers see a capable group strengthening the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the number recorded as part of the city’s repopulation. 1 Chronicles 9:6 gives a different group and number for Judah, a difference noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: These are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Joed, the son of Pedaiah, the son of Kolaiah, the son of Maaseiah, the son of Ithiel, the son of Jeshaiah.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Benjamin begin with Sallu son of Meshullam. Arminian readers see Benjamin taking its place in Jerusalem, alongside Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Benjamites listed, taking their place in the city alongside Judah. Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of who settled in Jerusalem.

verses.text: After him Gabbai and Sallai, nine hundred twenty-eight.
verses.arminianNotes: “After him Gabbai and Sallai, nine hundred twenty-eight.” Arminian readers see a substantial number of Benjamites joining the city’s population.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Benjamite total recorded. 1 Chronicles 9:9 gives nine hundred fifty-six for Benjamin, a difference noted rather than harmonized.

verses.text: Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel son of Zichri is overseer, and Judah son of Hassenuah is second over the city. Arminian readers see organized leadership established for the residents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see order in the city’s administration. The precise meaning of “second over the city” is uncertain, and readers in this tradition hold it loosely.

verses.text: Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin,
verses.arminianNotes: The priests begin with Jedaiah son of Joiarib and Jachin. Arminian readers see priestly families settling in Jerusalem to serve at God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priesthood represented as families settle in Jerusalem to serve at God’s house. Both traditions read the verse as a record of priestly presence in the city.

verses.text: Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Zadok, the son of Meraioth, the son of Ahitub, the ruler of God’s house,
verses.arminianNotes: Seraiah son of Hilkiah, “the ruler of God’s house,” is named with his ancestry. Arminian readers see a leading priest honored by his genealogy and role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priestly line and the ruler of God’s house named with his ancestry. Both traditions read the verse as honoring a leading priest’s place in the restored city.

verses.text: and their brothers who did the work of the house, eight hundred twenty-two; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pelaliah, the son of Amzi, the son of Zechariah, the son of Pashhur, the son of Malchijah,
verses.arminianNotes: Their brothers who did the work of the house number 822, and Adaiah’s line is given. Arminian readers see many priests devoted to the daily work of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see priestly service organized and recorded, with many devoted to the daily work of God’s house. Both traditions read the numbers as part of the city’s repopulation, without forcing agreement with parallel lists.

verses.text: and his brothers, chiefs of fathers’ households, two hundred forty-two; and Amashsai the son of Azarel, the son of Ahzai, the son of Meshillemoth, the son of Immer,
verses.arminianNotes: His brothers, chiefs of fathers’ households, number 242, and Amashsai’s line is traced to Immer. Arminian readers see family leadership supporting the priesthood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see family leadership supporting the priesthood. Both traditions read the verse as a record of household chiefs among the priests in Jerusalem.

verses.text: and their brothers, mighty men of valor, one hundred twenty-eight; and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of Haggedolim.
verses.arminianNotes: Their brothers, “mighty men of valor,” number 128, with Zabdiel as overseer. Arminian readers see strength and capability valued in temple service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see orderly oversight among the priests. Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of capable men serving in the house of God.

verses.text: Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Bunni;
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites begin with Shemaiah son of Hasshub. Arminian readers see Levitical families taking their place in Jerusalem to support worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites recorded as they take their place in Jerusalem to support worship. Both traditions read the verse as the start of the Levitical section of the list.

verses.text: and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chiefs of the Levites, who had the oversight of the outward business of God’s house;
verses.arminianNotes: Shabbethai and Jozabad oversee “the outward business of God’s house.” Arminian readers see practical administration recognized as part of serving God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites responsible for matters outside the sanctuary. Readers in this tradition value the reminder that external tasks also serve God’s house.

verses.text: and Mattaniah the son of Mica, the son of Zabdi, the son of Asaph, who was the chief to begin the thanksgiving in prayer, and Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers; and Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun.
verses.arminianNotes: Mattaniah of Asaph’s line is “the chief to begin the thanksgiving in prayer,” with Bakbukiah and Abda. Arminian readers see worship led by those devoted to thanksgiving.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the musicians’ role in leading praise and thanksgiving. Both traditions read the verse as a record of those appointed to begin the thanksgiving in prayer.

verses.text: All the Levites in the holy city were two hundred eighty-four.
verses.arminianNotes: “All the Levites in the holy city were two hundred eighty-four.” Arminian readers see the Levitical total recorded, showing a modest but committed group.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the number of Levites in the holy city noted. Both traditions read the total as showing a modest but committed group devoted to the service of God’s house.

verses.text: Moreover the gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were one hundred seventy-two.
verses.arminianNotes: The gatekeepers Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers number 172. Arminian readers see those who guarded the gates counted among the city’s residents.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the gatekeepers recorded among the city’s residents. Both traditions read the verse as part of the same careful list, without resolving differences from parallel notices.

verses.text: The residue of Israel, of the priests, and the Levites were in all the cities of Judah, everyone in his inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes: “The residue of Israel, of the priests, and the Levites were in all the cities of Judah, everyone in his inheritance.” Arminian readers see the rest of the people settled on their family land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the community distributed through the land. The verse balances the focus on Jerusalem with the wider settlement in Judah.

verses.text: But the temple servants lived in Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants.
verses.arminianNotes: The temple servants live in Ophel, with Ziha and Gishpa over them. Arminian readers see even the humblest servants given a place near God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the temple servants organized. The location of Ophel near the temple is commonly accepted, though readers in this tradition do not press precise boundaries.

verses.text: The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Mattaniah, the son of Mica, of the sons of Asaph, the singers responsible for the service of God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Uzzi of the sons of Asaph is overseer of the Levites, the singers responsible for the service of God’s house. Arminian readers see leadership among the musicians recognized.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the singers’ role honored. The genealogy links Uzzi with Mattaniah of verse 17, showing continuity among the families of musicians.

verses.text: For there was a commandment from the king concerning them, and a settled provision for the singers, as every day required.
verses.arminianNotes: “… there was a commandment from the king concerning them, and a settled provision for the singers.” Arminian readers see provision made for those who led worship daily.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see support given for the singers. The text does not specify which king is meant, and readers in this tradition do not assume an identification beyond what is stated.

verses.text: Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Pethahiah of the children of Zerah is “at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people.” Arminian readers see a representative serving between the people and the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see an official role connecting the community with royal authority. The exact nature of the position is not detailed, and readers in this tradition hold it loosely.
